claim: Global amphibian declines are compounded by deadly disease outbreaks caused by the chytrid fungus, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd).
source: Global amphibian declines are compounded by deadly disease outbreaks caused by the chytrid fungus, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about amphibian declines and chytrid fungus.

claim: Enrichment of X. laevis skin mast cells confers anti-Bd protection.
source: Our findings indicate that enrichment of X. laevis skin mast cells confers anti-Bd protection and ameliorates the inflammation-associated skin damage caused by Bd infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced Bd loads in mast cell-enriched animals.

claim: Mast cell enrichment ameliorates inflammation-associated skin damage caused by Bd infection.
source: Our findings indicate that enrichment of X. laevis skin mast cells confers anti-Bd protection and ameliorates the inflammation-associated skin damage caused by Bd infection.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations and measurements of epidermal thickness.

claim: Mast cell enrichment results in a significant reduction in infiltration of Bd-infected skin by neutrophils.
source: This includes a significant reduction in infiltration of Bd-infected skin by neutrophils, promoting mucin content within cutaneous mucus glands, and preventing Bd-mediated changes to skin microbiomes.
evidence: This is supported by mpo-positive cell counts in skin tissues.

claim: Mast cell enrichment promotes mucin content within cutaneous mucus glands.
source: This includes a significant reduction in infiltration of Bd-infected skin by neutrophils, promoting mucin content within cutaneous mucus glands, and preventing Bd-mediated changes to skin microbiomes.
evidence: This is supported by Alcian Blue/PAS staining showing increased mucus gland filling.

claim: Mast cell enrichment prevents Bd-mediated changes to skin microbiomes.
source: This includes a significant reduction in infiltration of Bd-infected skin by neutrophils, promoting mucin content within cutaneous mucus glands, and preventing Bd-mediated changes to skin microbiomes.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analyses showing less deviation in community composition.

claim: X. laevis IL4 plays a key role in manifesting the effects seen following cutaneous mast cell enrichment.
source: Mammalian mast cells are known for their production of the pleiotropic interleukin-4 (IL4) cytokine and our findings suggest that the X. laevis IL4 plays a key role in manifesting the effects seen following cutaneous mast cell enrichment.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that rIL4 administration recapitulates key protective effects.

claim: Catastrophic declines of hundreds of amphibian species across six continents have been causally linked to the chytrid fungi, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) and Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal).
source: Catastrophic declines of hundreds of amphibian species across six continents have been causally linked to the chytrid fungi, Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) and Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal) (Martel et al., 2014; Scheele et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Motile Bd zoospores readily colonize keratinized skin of adult amphibians and keratinized mouthparts of tadpoles.
source: Motile Bd zoospores readily colonize keratinized skin of adult amphibians and keratinized mouthparts of tadpoles (Van Rooij et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Bd skin infections culminate in chytridiomycosis, ultimately disrupting the function of this respiratory and barrier tissue.
source: Bd skin infections culminate in chytridiomycosis, ultimately disrupting the function of this respiratory and barrier tissue (Van Rooij et al., 2015; Van Rooij et al., 2010; Voyles et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The contribution of skin-resident immune cells to amphibian anti-Bd defenses remains almost entirely unexplored.
source: However, the contribution of skin-resident immune cells to amphibian anti-Bd defenses remains almost entirely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Mammalian mast cells serve as sentinels of mucosal and connective tissues, including in barrier tissues like skin, where they maintain homeostasis and regulate immune responses.
source: Mammalian mast cells serve as sentinels of mucosal and connective tissues, including in barrier tissues like skin, where they maintain homeostasis and regulate immune responses (Sobiepanek et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mast cells are among the first immune cells to recognize and respond to skin-infiltrating pathogens.
source: Consequently, mast cells are among the first immune cells to recognize and respond to skin-infiltrating pathogens.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that mast cells reside in tissues while neutrophils are recruited during inflammation.

claim: When activated, mast cells release pre-formed and de novo-generated immunomodulatory compounds that may serve to elicit, exacerbate, or ameliorate inflammatory responses.
source: When activated, mast cells release pre-formed and de novo-generated immunomodulatory compounds that may serve to elicit, exacerbate, or ameliorate inflammatory responses (Sobiepanek et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The interleukin-4 (IL4) cytokine dampens inflammation and promotes tissue repair.
source: One of these mast cell-produced mediators, the interleukin-4 (IL4) cytokine dampens inflammation and promotes tissue repair (Allen, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Cells bearing hallmark mast cell cytology have been reported across a range of non-mammalian species.
source: Cells bearing hallmark mast cell cytology have been reported across a range of non-mammalian species (McNeil et al., 2007; Abraham and St John, 2010), including amphibians (Baccari et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The principal mast cell growth factor, stem cell factor (SCF, KIT ligand), is required for mast cell differentiation and survival.
source: Notably, the principal mast cell growth factor, stem cell factor (SCF, KIT ligand), is required for mast cell differentiation and survival (Ito et al., 2012) and is expressed by all vertebrates examined to date.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: SCF is expressed by all vertebrates examined to date.
source: Notably, the principal mast cell growth factor, stem cell factor (SCF, KIT ligand), is required for mast cell differentiation and survival (Ito et al., 2012) and is expressed by all vertebrates examined to date.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on existing knowledge.

claim: X. laevis mast cell cultures consist predominantly of mononuclear cells with basophilic cytoplasm.
source: While the neutrophil cultures were comprised of cells with hyper-segmented nuclei and neutral-staining cytoplasms (Figure 1A), the mast cell cultures consisted predominantly of mononuclear cells with basophilic cytoplasm (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Giemsa staining shown in Figure 1B.

claim: X. laevis neutrophil cultures are comprised of cells with hyper-segmented nuclei and neutral-staining cytoplasms.
source: While the neutrophil cultures were comprised of cells with hyper-segmented nuclei and neutral-staining cytoplasms (Figure 1A), the mast cell cultures consisted predominantly of mononuclear cells with basophilic cytoplasm (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Giemsa staining shown in Figure 1A.

claim: X. laevis mast cells are specific esterase (SE)-positive.
source: We confirmed the granulocyte-lineage of X. laevis mast cells using specific esterase (SE) staining (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by SE staining shown in Figure 1D.

claim: X. laevis neutrophils are SE-positive.
source: As expected, X. laevis neutrophils were also SE-positive (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by SE staining shown in Figure 1C.

claim: X. laevis mast cells possess extensive folding of their plasma membranes.
source: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging demonstrated that X. laevis mast cells possess extensive folding of their plasma membranes (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1F.

claim: X. laevis mast cells possess electron-dense heterogeneous granules, few mitochondria, and round to elongated nuclei.
source: This mast cell-characteristic membrane ruffling appeared as projections resembling pseudopods via transmission electron microscopy (TEM), which further revealed electron-dense heterogeneous granules, few mitochondria, and round to elongated nuclei (Figure 1H) typical of mammalian mast cells (Espinosa-Riquer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by TEM imaging shown in Figure 1H.

claim: X. laevis neutrophils exhibit pronounced membrane ruffling.
source: X. laevis neutrophils also exhibited pronounced membrane ruffling (Figure 1E) but strikingly distinct intracellular appearance including multilobed nuclei (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by SEM imaging shown in Figure 1E.

claim: X. laevis neutrophils have multilobed nuclei.
source: X. laevis neutrophils also exhibited pronounced membrane ruffling (Figure 1E) but strikingly distinct intracellular appearance including multilobed nuclei (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by TEM imaging shown in Figure 1G.

claim: X. laevis mast cells and neutrophils exhibit distinct transcriptional profiles of immune-related genes.
source: X. laevis mast cells and neutrophils exhibited distinct transcriptional profiles of immune-related genes including those encoding lineage-specific transcription factors, immune receptors, downstream signaling components and adhesion molecules, as well as non-immune genes (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Frog mast cells express greater levels of lineage-specific transcription factors gata1, gata2, and mitf compared to neutrophils.
source: Frog mast cells and neutrophils each expressed greater levels of lineage-specific transcription factors associated with mammalian mast cell (gata1, gata2, and mitf) (Cildir et al., 2021) and neutrophil (cebp family members) (Paudel et al., 2022) counterparts, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Frog neutrophils express greater levels of cebp family transcription factors compared to mast cells.
source: Frog mast cells and neutrophils each expressed greater levels of lineage-specific transcription factors associated with mammalian mast cell (gata1, gata2, and mitf) (Cildir et al., 2021) and neutrophil (cebp family members) (Paudel et al., 2022) counterparts, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mast cells express greater levels of carboxypeptidase-3 (cpa3) gene associated with tissue remodeling.
source: Notably, mast cells expressed greater levels of enzyme and cytokine genes associated with tissue remodeling (carboxypeptidase-3 [cpa3]; Atiakshin et al., 2022), immune suppression (indoleamine 2,3 dioxygenase-1 [ido1]; Baban et al., 2009), and amelioration of cutaneous inflammation (leukemia inhibitory factor [lif]; Banner et al., 1998; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B and cited literature.

claim: Mast cells express greater levels of indoleamine 2,3 dioxygenase-1 (ido1) gene associated with immune suppression.
source: Notably, mast cells expressed greater levels of enzyme and cytokine genes associated with tissue remodeling (carboxypeptidase-3 [cpa3]; Atiakshin et al., 2022), immune suppression (indoleamine 2,3 dioxygenase-1 [ido1]; Baban et al., 2009), and amelioration of cutaneous inflammation (leukemia inhibitory factor [lif]; Banner et al., 1998; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B and cited literature.

claim: Mast cells express greater levels of leukemia inhibitory factor (lif) gene associated with amelioration of cutaneous inflammation.
source: Notably, mast cells expressed greater levels of enzyme and cytokine genes associated with tissue remodeling (carboxypeptidase-3 [cpa3]; Atiakshin et al., 2022), immune suppression (indoleamine 2,3 dioxygenase-1 [ido1]; Baban et al., 2009), and amelioration of cutaneous inflammation (leukemia inhibitory factor [lif]; Banner et al., 1998; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B and cited literature.

claim: Neutrophils express predominantly proinflammatory enzymes and cytokine genes such as leukotriene 4 hydrolase (lta4h) and tumor necrosis factor alpha (tnfa).
source: Conversely, neutrophils expressed predominantly proinflammatory enzymes and cytokine genes such as leukotriene 4 hydrolase (lta4h; Figure 2B) and tumor necrosis factor alpha (tnfa, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mast cells have greater expression of kit gene encoding their growth factor receptor.
source: In addition, mast cells and neutrophils each had greater expression of genes encoding their respective growth factor receptors, kit and csf3r (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Neutrophils have greater expression of csf3r gene encoding their growth factor receptor.
source: In addition, mast cells and neutrophils each had greater expression of genes encoding their respective growth factor receptors, kit and csf3r (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Subcutaneous rSCF administration enriches mast cells in X. laevis skin.
source: Therefore, we selectively enriched mast cells in X. laevis skin via subcutaneous rSCF administration (note SE-stained cells indicated by arrows in r-ctrl-injected skins, Figure 3A, versus r-SCF-injected skins, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by SE staining shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: SE-positive cells in rSCF-treated skins possess round-oval nuclei.
source: We confirmed SE-positive cells in rSCF-treated skins also possessed round-oval nuclei (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Maximum mast cell enrichment was observed 12 hr post injection of rSCF.
source: Maximum mast cell enrichment was observed 12 hr post injection of rSCF (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At 10 dpi, skin mast cell-enriched X. laevis possessed significantly lower Bd loads than r-ctrl-administered animals.
source: At 10 dpi, skin mast cell-enriched X. laevis possessed significantly lower Bd loads than r-ctrl-administered animals (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: By 21 dpi, mast cell-enriched animals continued to show significantly lower skin fungal loads compared to control animals.
source: By 21 dpi, both r-ctrl and rSCF-administered groups possessed substantially greater Bd loads, although the mast cell-enriched animals continued to show significantly lower skin fungal loads (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Frog bone marrow-derived mast cells possess heparin-containing granules.
source: Using this approach, we confirmed that frog bone marrow-derived mast cells likewise possess heparin-containing granules (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by avidin staining shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Cutaneous frog mast cell enrichment progressively waned with time in mock-infected animals.
source: We observed cutaneous frog mast cell enrichment progressively waned with time in mock-infected animals, and by 21 days post mock infection, these animals had skin mast cell numbers comparable to r-ctrl-injected, mock-infected animals (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by avidin staining and quantification shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: rSCF-injected, Bd-challenged frogs maintained significantly more cutaneous mast cells numbers throughout the 21-day infection study compared to mock-infected control animals.
source: Conversely, compared to mock-infected control animals, the rSCF-injected, Bd-challenged frogs maintained significantly more cutaneous mast cells numbers throughout the 21-day infection study (Figure 4C and E–H).
evidence: This is supported by avidin staining and quantification shown in Figures 4C and 4E-H.

claim: r-ctrl-injected, Bd-infected animals exhibited significantly increased skin mast cell numbers at 10 and 21 days of infection compared to uninfected control frogs.
source: Interestingly, r-ctrl-injected, Bd-infected animals exhibited significantly increased skin mast cell numbers at 10 and 21 days of infection compared to uninfected control frogs (Figure 4C and I).
evidence: This is supported by avidin staining and quantification shown in Figures 4C and 4I.

claim: Most mast cells in Bd-infected skin were observed in the epidermal layer, spreading out between the skin epithelial cells.
source: Most of these mast cells were observed in the epidermal layer, spreading out between the skin epithelial cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Mast cell-enriched, Bd-infected skins possessed more transcripts for genes associated with cutaneous strength and integrity (lamc2).
source: Among the top differentially expressed genes, we noted mast cell-enriched, Bd-infected skins possessed more transcripts for genes associated with cutaneous strength and integrity (lamc2) (Kiritsi et al., 2013), suppression of cell migration (b3gnt3.1) (Ho et al., 2013), as well as ion and nutrient flow (gjb3l) (Chang et al., 2003; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and cited literature.

claim: Mast cell-enriched Bd-challenged skin exhibited greater expression of genes associated with protection of the mucosa and epithelial healing (ttf3.6s).
source: Moreover, mast cell-enriched Bd-challenged skin exhibited greater expression of genes associated with protection of the mucosa and epithelial healing (ttf3.6s) (Taupin and Podolsky, 2003) and mucus production (duoxa1.s [Fischer, 2009], gabrp [Wang et al., 2021]; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and cited literature.

claim: Skins from control Bd-infected frogs revealed greater expression of genes associated with leukocyte infiltration and inflammation (e.g., ccl19, cxcl16, adamts13, csf3r).
source: In striking contrast, skins from control Bd-infected frogs revealed greater expression of genes associated with leukocyte infiltration and inflammation (e.g., ccl19, cxcl16, adamts13, csf3r; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Control (r-ctrl), Bd-infected skins exhibited hyperkeratosis, epidermal hyperplasia, jagged stratum corneum, and extensive leukocyte infiltration.
source: These transcriptional profiles were supported by our histological observations wherein control (r-ctrl), Bd-infected skins exhibited hyperkeratosis, epidermal hyperplasia, jagged stratum corneum, and extensive leukocyte infiltration (Figure 5B), while mast cell-enriched Bd-infected tissues appeared considerably less afflicted by these pathologies (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mast cell-enriched Bd-infected tissues appeared considerably less afflicted by pathologies compared to control Bd-infected skins.
source: These transcriptional profiles were supported by our histological observations wherein control (r-ctrl), Bd-infected skins exhibited hyperkeratosis, epidermal hyperplasia, jagged stratum corneum, and extensive leukocyte infiltration (Figure 5B), while mast cell-enriched Bd-infected tissues appeared considerably less afflicted by these pathologies (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mast cell-enriched animals possessed significantly less thickened epidermal skin compared to control (r-ctrl), Bd-infected animals.
source: Quantification of Bd-infected skin thickness confirmed that mast cell-enriched animals possessed significantly less thickened epidermal skin compared to control (r-ctrl), Bd-infected animals (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cutaneous mucus glands of mast cell-enriched, mock- and Bd-infected frogs were significantly more filled than those of mock- and Bd-infected control animals.
source: Interestingly, cutaneous mucus glands of mast cell-enriched, mock- and Bd-infected frogs were significantly more filled than those of mock- and Bd-infected control animals (Figure 5B, C, and E).
evidence: This is supported by Alcian Blue/PAS staining and quantification shown in Figures 5B, 5C, and 5E.

claim: All vertebrate neutrophils depend on CSF3 for their differentiation and function.
source: All vertebrate neutrophils depend on CSF3 for their differentiation and function (Roberts, 2005), and our previous work has confirmed that this is true of frog neutrophils, which intuitively also exhibit high expression the CSF3 receptor (csf3r) (Koubourli et al., 2017; Yaparla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Frog neutrophils exhibit high expression of the CSF3 receptor (csf3r).
source: All vertebrate neutrophils depend on CSF3 for their differentiation and function (Roberts, 2005), and our previous work has confirmed that this is true of frog neutrophils, which intuitively also exhibit high expression the CSF3 receptor (csf3r) (Koubourli et al., 2017; Yaparla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: The skins of r-ctrl-injected, Bd-infected animals had significantly elevated neutrophil numbers at 10 and 21 dpi.
source: While the skins of r-ctrl- and rSCF-administered, mock-infected frogs contained relatively few neutrophils (Figure 6A and E), the skins of r-ctrl-injected, Bd-infected animals had significantly elevated neutrophil numbers (Figure 6B, C, and E).
evidence: This is supported by RNAScope analysis of mpo shown in Figures 6B, 6C, and 6E.

claim: At both 10 and 21 dpi, the skins of mast cell-enriched frogs possessed neutrophil levels similar to those seen in the uninfected animals.
source: Conversely, at both examined time points (10, 21 dpi), the skins of mast cell-enriched frogs possessed neutrophil levels similar to those seen in the uninfected animals (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by RNAScope analysis of mpo shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Subcutaneous rCSF3 administration results in neutrophil enrichment in frog skin.
source: We next assessed the consequence of enriching frog skins for neutrophils via subcutaneous rCSF3 administration. We confirmed neutrophil enrichment peaked 12 hp rCSF3 injection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and resulted in a thickened epidermis in comparison with r-ctrl-injected skins of otherwise healthy animals (i.e., no Bd; Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by SE staining shown in Figures 6F and 6G and time course data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When challenged with Bd, frogs with neutrophil-enriched skin possessed significantly greater Bd loads than control frogs.
source: When challenged with Bd, frogs with neutrophil-enriched skin possessed significantly greater Bd loads than control frogs (Figure 6H), suggesting that neutrophil-mediated inflammation may be exacerbating Bd infections.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Neutrophil-mediated inflammation may be exacerbating Bd infections.
source: When challenged with Bd, frogs with neutrophil-enriched skin possessed significantly greater Bd loads than control frogs (Figure 6H), suggesting that neutrophil-mediated inflammation may be exacerbating Bd infections.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neutrophil enrichment increases Bd loads.

claim: A total of 1645 bacterial amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were identified from 20 bacterial phyla.
source: A total of 1645 bacterial amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were identified from 20 bacterial phyla, 7 of which were predominant (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by microbiome sequencing data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Verrucomicrobiota were only present on uninfected animals.
source: Of these, Verrucomicrobiota were only present on uninfected animals, whereas Acidobacteriota was only seen after 21 dpi on both control and mast cell-enriched, infected animals (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Acidobacteriota was only seen after 21 dpi on both control and mast cell-enriched, infected animals.
source: Of these, Verrucomicrobiota were only present on uninfected animals, whereas Acidobacteriota was only seen after 21 dpi on both control and mast cell-enriched, infected animals (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by microbiome data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At 10 dpi, mast cell enrichment resulted in a nominal shift in community composition compared to control frogs.
source: At 10 dpi, mast cell enrichment resulted in a nominal shift in community composition compared to control frogs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Control, Bd-infected animals exhibited a drastic shift in community composition at 10 dpi.
source: Notably, while control, Bd-infected animals exhibited a drastic shift in community composition, mast cell-enriched animals possessed substantially less deviated community composition (Figure 7B), suggesting that these cells are somehow counteracting the adverse effects of Bd on the X. laevis cutaneous microbiome communities.
evidence: This is supported by PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mast cell-enriched animals possessed substantially less deviated community composition compared to control Bd-infected animals at 10 dpi.
source: Notably, while control, Bd-infected animals exhibited a drastic shift in community composition, mast cell-enriched animals possessed substantially less deviated community composition (Figure 7B), suggesting that these cells are somehow counteracting the adverse effects of Bd on the X. laevis cutaneous microbiome communities.
evidence: This is supported by PERMANOVA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mast cells are counteracting the adverse effects of Bd on the X. laevis cutaneous microbiome communities.
source: Notably, while control, Bd-infected animals exhibited a drastic shift in community composition, mast cell-enriched animals possessed substantially less deviated community composition (Figure 7B), suggesting that these cells are somehow counteracting the adverse effects of Bd on the X. laevis cutaneous microbiome communities.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mast cell enrichment prevents Bd-mediated microbiome changes.

claim: At 10 dpi, mast cell-enriched and mock-infected frogs possessed significantly greater abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria such as Chryseobacterium sp. compared to control, mock-infected animals.
source: At 10 dpi, mast cell-enriched and mock-infected frogs possessed significantly greater abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria such as Chryseobacterium sp. (Woodhams, 2015), compared to control, mock-infected animals (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis shown in Figure 7C and cited literature.

claim: Mast cells may promote skin flora composition that is more antifungal.
source: This suggests mast cells may promote skin flora composition that is more antifungal.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mast cell-enriched animals have greater abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria.

claim: Control (non-enriched) Bd-infected frogs possessed significantly greater abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria than all other treatment groups at 10 dpi.
source: Control (non-enriched) Bd-infected frogs possessed significantly greater abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria than all other treatment groups (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Mast cell-enriched uninfected frogs exhibited increased skin bacterial richness at 10 dpi.
source: Mast cell-enriched uninfected frogs exhibited increased skin bacterial richness at 10 dpi (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Control Bd-infected animals exhibited significantly reduced skin microbial richness at 10 dpi.
source: While control Bd-infected animals exhibited significantly reduced skin microbial richness, mast cell-enriched Bd-infected frogs did not exhibit such a reduction in bacterial richness (Figure 7D), supporting the idea that mast cells may be counteracting the adverse effects of Bd on skin microbiome composition.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Mast cell-enriched Bd-infected frogs did not exhibit a reduction in bacterial richness at 10 dpi.
source: While control Bd-infected animals exhibited significantly reduced skin microbial richness, mast cell-enriched Bd-infected frogs did not exhibit such a reduction in bacterial richness (Figure 7D), supporting the idea that mast cells may be counteracting the adverse effects of Bd on skin microbiome composition.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There were no significant differences in direct Bd-killing capacities of mucus isolated from mock- or Bd-challenged control or mast cell-enriched frogs.
source: However, we found no significant differences in direct Bd-killing capacities of mucus isolated from mock- or Bd-challenged control or mast cell-enriched frogs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by mucosome killing assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bd-challenged mast cells upregulated their expression of the AMP-encoding genes, PGLa (pgla) and magainin (mag).
source: As anticipated, Bd-challenged mast cells, but not Bd-challenged neutrophils, upregulated their expression of the AMP-encoding genes, PGLa (pgla) and magainin (mag, Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Bd-challenged neutrophils did not upregulate their expression of PGLa (pgla) and magainin (mag).
source: As anticipated, Bd-challenged mast cells, but not Bd-challenged neutrophils, upregulated their expression of the AMP-encoding genes, PGLa (pgla) and magainin (mag, Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: After 10 days of mock infection, mast cell-enriched animals possessed significantly greater skin expression of mag and pgla than control animals.
source: Conversely, after 10 days of mock infection, mast cell-enriched animals possessed significantly greater skin expression of mag and pgla than control animals (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: X. laevis mast cells challenged in vitro with Bd significantly upregulated their il4 gene expression.
source: Notably, X. laevis mast cells challenged in vitro with Bd significantly upregulated their il4 gene expression, whereas almost no il4 expression was detected from either unstimulated or Bd-challenged neutrophils (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Almost no il4 expression was detected from either unstimulated or Bd-challenged neutrophils.
source: Notably, X. laevis mast cells challenged in vitro with Bd significantly upregulated their il4 gene expression, whereas almost no il4 expression was detected from either unstimulated or Bd-challenged neutrophils (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 12 hr following rSCF administration, the mast cell-enriched frog skins possessed significantly greater transcripts of il4 than control animals.
source: When we examined the expression of il4 in the skin of control and mast cell-enriched animals, we found that 12 hr following rSCF administration (time of Bd challenge), the mast cell-enriched frog skins possessed significantly greater transcripts of il4 than control animals (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: At 10 days of Bd infection, mast cell-enriched frog skins had significantly elevated il4 transcript levels.
source: At 10 days of Bd infection, control animals possessed increased (not significantly) skin il4 gene expression whereas mast cell-enriched frog skins had significantly elevated il4 transcript levels (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Subcutaneous injection of rIL4 augmented expression of genes known to be activated by the mammalian IL4 (cd36, metalloproteinase inhibitor 3-timp3, and monoamine oxidase A-maoa).
source: To examine whether IL4 could confer the anti-Bd effects seen following frog skin mast cell enrichment, we produced this X. laevis cytokine in recombinant form (rIL4) and confirmed that subcutaneous injection of rIL4 augmented expression of genes known to be activated by the mammalian IL4 (Bhattacharjee et al., 2013) (cd36, metalloproteinase inhibitor 3-timp3, and monoamine oxidase A-maoa; Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and cited literature.

claim: Frogs treated with rIL4 possessed greater skin mucus gland filling than control animals, irrespective of mock- or Bd-challenge.
source: When we examined the mucus content of control and rIL4-administered animals, we found that frogs treated with rIL4 possessed greater skin mucus gland filling than control animals, irrespective of mock- or Bd-challenge (Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This is supported by Alcian Blue/PAS staining and quantification shown in Figures 8C-E.

claim: At 21 dpi, rIL4-administered frogs possessed significantly lower skin Bd loads.
source: At 21 dpi (but not at 10 dpi), rIL4-administered frogs possessed significantly lower skin Bd loads (Figure 8F), exhibited significantly less epidermal thickening (Figure 8C, D, and G) and less neutrophil infiltration (Figure 8H–J) than control infected animals.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: At 21 dpi, rIL4-administered frogs exhibited significantly less epidermal thickening than control infected animals.
source: At 21 dpi (but not at 10 dpi), rIL4-administered frogs possessed significantly lower skin Bd loads (Figure 8F), exhibited significantly less epidermal thickening (Figure 8C, D, and G) and less neutrophil infiltration (Figure 8H–J) than control infected animals.
evidence: This is supported by histological measurements shown in Figures 8C, 8D, and 8G.

claim: At 21 dpi, rIL4-administered frogs had less neutrophil infiltration than control infected animals.
source: At 21 dpi (but not at 10 dpi), rIL4-administered frogs possessed significantly lower skin Bd loads (Figure 8F), exhibited significantly less epidermal thickening (Figure 8C, D, and G) and less neutrophil infiltration (Figure 8H–J) than control infected animals.
evidence: This is supported by RNAScope analysis shown in Figures 8H-J.

claim: Subcutaneous administration of rIL4 to animals with active Bd-infection did not alter their fungal loads.
source: Conversely, subcutaneous administration of rIL4 to animals with active Bd-infection did not alter their fungal loads (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), suggesting a critical point during which IL4 may offer protection against this fungal pathogen.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There is a critical point during which IL4 may offer protection against Bd.
source: Conversely, subcutaneous administration of rIL4 to animals with active Bd-infection did not alter their fungal loads (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B), suggesting a critical point during which IL4 may offer protection against this fungal pathogen.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IL4 is protective when given before but not during active infection.

claim: Amphibian extinction rates far outpace those of any other vertebrate class.
source: Amphibian extinction rates far outpace those of any other vertebrate class (IUCN 2022, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to IUCN data.

claim: Chytrid fungi are considered the greatest infectious disease threat to biodiversity.
source: It is now well established that chytrid fungi are major contributors to these declines, and strikingly, are considered the greatest infectious disease threat to biodiversity (Fisher and Garner, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mammalian mast cells are potent producers of the pleotropic anti-inflammatory interleukin-4 (IL4) cytokine.
source: Mammalian mast cells are potent producers of the pleotropic anti-inflammatory interleukin-4 (IL4) (Babina et al., 2016) cytokine, and our findings suggest that this is also true of frog mast cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Frog mast cells are potent producers of IL4.
source: Mammalian mast cells are potent producers of the pleotropic anti-inflammatory interleukin-4 (IL4) (Babina et al., 2016) cytokine, and our findings suggest that this is also true of frog mast cells.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data showing il4 upregulation in Bd-challenged mast cells.

claim: In mammals, IL4 plays roles in tissue repair.
source: In mammals, IL4 also plays roles in tissue repair (Allen, 2023) and mucus production by intestinal goblet cells (Redpath et al., 2015), which aids in the 'weep and sweep' pathogen elimination and may contribute to the maintenance of commensal communities in the gut (Drago et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In mammals, IL4 plays roles in mucus production by intestinal goblet cells.
source: In mammals, IL4 also plays roles in tissue repair (Allen, 2023) and mucus production by intestinal goblet cells (Redpath et al., 2015), which aids in the 'weep and sweep' pathogen elimination and may contribute to the maintenance of commensal communities in the gut (Drago et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: IL4 may be a central means by which frog mast cells confer protection against Bd by counteracting Bd-elicited inflammation.
source: This is consistent with our findings, which suggest that IL4 may be a central means by which frog mast cells confer protection against Bd by counteracting Bd-elicited inflammation, including minimizing neutrophil infiltration, maintaining skin integrity, and promoting mucus production by skin mucus glands.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rIL4 administration recapitulates protective effects of mast cell enrichment.

claim: Bd infections caused major reductions in bacterial taxa richness.
source: Bd infections caused major reductions in bacterial taxa richness, changes in composition and substantial increases in the relative abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria early in the infection.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis data.

claim: Bd infections caused changes in microbiome composition.
source: Bd infections caused major reductions in bacterial taxa richness, changes in composition and substantial increases in the relative abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria early in the infection.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis data.

claim: Bd infections caused substantial increases in the relative abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria early in the infection.
source: Bd infections caused major reductions in bacterial taxa richness, changes in composition and substantial increases in the relative abundance of Bd-inhibitory bacteria early in the infection.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis data.

claim: Similar changes to microbiome structure occur during experimental Bd infections in red-backed salamanders and mountain yellow-legged frogs.
source: Similar changes to microbiome structure occur during experimental Bd infections, such as in red-backed salamanders and mountain yellow-legged frogs (Jani et al., 2021; Muletz-Wolz et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Progressing Bd infections corresponded with a return to baseline levels of Bd-inhibitory bacteria abundance and rebounding microbial richness.
source: In turn, progressing Bd infections corresponded with a return to baseline levels of Bd-inhibitory bacteria abundance and rebounding microbial richness, albeit with dissimilar communities to those seen in control animals.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis data.

claim: Amphibian microbiomes are dynamic.
source: These temporal changes indicate that amphibian microbiomes are dynamic, as are the effects of Bd infections on them.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of temporal changes in microbiome structure.

claim: Bd infections may have long-lasting impacts on amphibian microbiomes.
source: Indeed, Bd infections may have long-lasting impacts on amphibian microbiomes (Jani et al., 2021), including the possible establishment of 'ecological memory', resulting in greater adaptation to subsequent pathogen exposures (Woodhams et al., 2023; Letourneau et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Mast cell enrichment appeared to counteract the deleterious effects of Bd on frog skin microbiome structure.
source: While Bd infections manifested in these considerable changes to frog skin microbiome structure, mast cell enrichment appeared to counteract these deleterious effects to skin microbial composition.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis data showing less deviation in mast cell-enriched animals.

claim: Mast cell-mediated mucus production and preservation of skin integrity stabilizes the cutaneous microenvironment during Bd infections.
source: Presumably, mast cell-mediated mucus production and preservation of skin integrity stabilizes the cutaneous microenvironment during Bd infections, thereby ameliorating the Bd-mediated microbiome changes.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed effects of mast cells on mucus production and skin integrity.

claim: Mammalian skin mast cell functionality depends on microbiome elicited SCF production by keratinocytes.
source: Intriguingly, while mammalian skin mast cell functionality depends on microbiome elicited SCF production by keratinocytes (Wang et al., 2017), our results indicate frog skin mast cells in turn impact skin microbiome structure and likely their function.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Frog skin mast cells impact skin microbiome structure and likely their function.
source: Intriguingly, while mammalian skin mast cell functionality depends on microbiome elicited SCF production by keratinocytes (Wang et al., 2017), our results indicate frog skin mast cells in turn impact skin microbiome structure and likely their function.
evidence: This is supported by microbiome analysis data showing mast cell effects on microbiome composition.

claim: Enrichment of neutrophils resulted in greater Bd burdens on frog skins.
source: In contrast to the protective effects conferred by mast cell enrichment, enrichment of neutrophils resulted in greater Bd burdens on frog skins.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data showing increased Bd loads in neutrophil-enriched animals.

claim: Neutrophils may lead to heightened inflammation, which is not protective in the context of Bd infections.
source: This suggests neutrophils may lead to heightened inflammation, which is not protective in the context of Bd infections.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neutrophil enrichment increases Bd loads.

claim: Robust immune responses may be counterproductive to amphibian anti-Bd defenses.
source: This is consistent with other studies indicating that robust immune responses may be counterproductive to amphibian anti-Bd defenses (Ellison et al., 2014; Savage et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Amphibian skin is much thinner and more permeable than those of mammals.
source: Amphibian skin is much thinner and more permeable than those of mammals (Varga et al., 2018), and as such, arguably represents a more penetrable barrier to pathogens.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mammalian mast cells are absent from healthy mammalian epidermises and are instead found exclusively in their dermal layers.
source: Because mammalian skin is relatively impermeable, mast cells are absent from healthy mammalian epidermises and are instead found exclusively in their dermal layers (Cowen et al., 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mammalian mast cells may infiltrate the skin epidermal layer during diseases such as dermatitis.
source: However, mammalian mast cells may infiltrate the skin epidermal layer during diseases such as dermatitis (Imayama et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mast cells are found in both epidermal and dermal layers of amphibian skin.
source: We have shown here and have observed across several classes of amphibians (Hauser et al., 2023) that mast cells are found in both epidermal and dermal layers.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations and cited work.

claim: Amphibian skin-resident mast cells likely coevolved to support skin immunity, physiology, and symbiotic microbiota.
source: Considering the importance of amphibian cutaneous integrity to their physiology (Larsen, 2021), it is likely that skin-resident mast cells coevolved to support skin immunity, physiology, and symbiotic microbiota.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed roles of mast cells in skin immunity and microbiome regulation.

claim: There are functional differences between mammalian connective tissue and mucosa-resident mast cells.
source: Ongoing research continues to reveal functional differences between mammalian connective tissue and mucosa-resident mast cells (West and Bulfone-Paus, 2022), and we suspect that there is similarly much to learn about the distinct physiological and immune roles of amphibian epidermal and dermal mast cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mammalian mast cells are thought to arise from two distinct lineages.
source: Mammalian mast cells are thought to arise from two distinct lineages. Fetal-derived progenitors seed peripheral tissues during the neonatal life (Gentek et al., 2018) and mature into long-lived connective tissue mast cells (CTMCs) (Dwyer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Inducible mucosal mast cells (MMCs) arise from bone marrow-derived mast cell progenitors (MCps) and are recruited to mucosal tissues in response to inflammation.
source: Conversely, inducible mucosal mast cells (MMCs) arise from bone marrow-derived mast cell progenitors (MCps) and are recruited to mucosal tissues in response to inflammation (Bankova et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Connective tissue mast cells are thought to possess significantly greater levels of heparin than bone marrow-derived mast cells.
source: The connective tissue mast cells are thought to possess significantly greater levels of heparin than bone marrow-derived mast cells (Herrera-Heredia et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: In vitro frog bone marrow-derived mast cells possessed substantially lower heparin content than what was observed in the skin-resident and Bd-elicited mast cells.
source: Interestingly, the in vitro frog bone marrow-derived mast cells possessed substantially lower heparin content than what we observed in the skin-resident and Bd-elicited mast cells.
evidence: This is supported by avidin staining data comparing in vitro and in vivo mast cells.

claim: Amphibian host-Bd interactions are highly complex and multifaceted.
source: It has become apparent that amphibian host-Bd interactions are highly complex and multifaceted and susceptibilities to this devastating pathogen markedly differ across amphibian species (Scheele et al., 2019; Van Rooij et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Susceptibilities to Bd markedly differ across amphibian species.
source: It has become apparent that amphibian host-Bd interactions are highly complex and multifaceted and susceptibilities to this devastating pathogen markedly differ across amphibian species (Scheele et al., 2019; Van Rooij et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Skin-resident mast cells are important for successful anti-Bd defenses.
source: The findings described here emphasize the importance of skin-resident mast cells for successful anti-Bd defenses and demonstrate that these immune sentinels are intimately linked to many aspects of frog skin physiology.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing protective effects of mast cell enrichment.

claim: Mast cells are intimately linked to many aspects of frog skin physiology.
source: The findings described here emphasize the importance of skin-resident mast cells for successful anti-Bd defenses and demonstrate that these immune sentinels are intimately linked to many aspects of frog skin physiology.
evidence: This is supported by the observed effects of mast cells on mucus production, skin integrity, and microbiome composition.

claim: When mast cells are enriched, the ensuing changes in the skin allow for greater resistance to Bd infection.
source: Our results indicate that when mast cells are enriched, the ensuing changes in the skin allow for greater resistance to Bd infection.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing reduced Bd loads in mast cell-enriched animals.

claim: Species-specific differences in mast cell function may contribute to the disparate susceptibilities of distinct amphibian species to pathogens like chytrid fungi.
source: Presumably, distinct amphibian species have evolved disparate interconnections between their skin mast cells and their cutaneous defenses, as dictated by their respective physiological and environmental pressures. In turn, these species-specific differences likely dictate whether and to what extent the skin-resident mast cells of a given amphibian species recognize and appropriately respond to Bd infections. We postulate that such differences may contribute to the disparate susceptibilities of distinct amphibian species to pathogens like chytrid fungi.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed importance of mast cells in anti-Bd defenses.
